## The question, frozen

The document answers several questions at once. **Frozen here is the one its title and opening make central**: *What force moves the nations?* — stated in Chapter I ("what is the power that moves peoples?"), and set as the test of all history at the end of Chapter III. Range: the great movements of peoples — the Crusades, the migration of peoples, 1789 to 1815. Kind of question: forward ("what produces it?"), with a rule-question hanging off it ("what does the word 'power' mean?"). Written down as new questions, not tested here: *is the will free?* (Ch. VIII–IX) and *why did 1789 turn west-to-east and back?* I worked from the method's own words, as the source theory file is not in front of me.

## The explanation in parts

1. The ancients said God directs a chosen man's will to predestined ends.
2. Modern history rejects that in words but keeps it in practice: nations led by individuals, and a known aim.
3. Power is not the wielder's physical or moral strength (Louis XI, Metternich ruled millions with no special qualities).
4. The jurists' answer: the people's will transferred to rulers by consent.
5. Three classes of historians all restate the question — "power is power."
6. No command causes the event; only the commands that match the course of events are executed.
7. The cone: in an army, and in any administration, the more directly a man acts, the less he commands and the more there are of him.
8. Power is the relation in which the more a man gives opinions, predictions and justifications of the action, the less he shares in it.
9. The movement of nations is caused by the activity of all who take part, not by power or ideas.
10. So "cause" does not apply; it is a law, "inconceivable otherwise."
11. The locomotive: a force commensurate with the movement is the only kind that could explain it.
12. Justifications arrive ahead of events and lift moral responsibility (the broom, the bow-wave).
13. The herd follows its head animal; the pasturage and the driver are ignored.
14. History studies our presentation of the will, so law and freedom do not clash.
15. The naturalists are plasterers smoothing one wall of a church.

## Part by part

| Part | Mark |
|---|---|
| 1 God directs the chosen man | **Borrowed** — on theology, not tested here; he says it is dead |
| 2 Modern history keeps the two assumptions | **Held** — by the survey from Gibbon to Buckle; the aim and the leader can be named in each |
| 3 Not strength or genius | **Held** — Louis XI, Metternich; this kills the genius version |
| 4 The jurists' consent-transfer | **Held** — by Pugachëv, by Napoleon III at Boulogne, by palace revolutions; it forces the search into the relation |
| 5 Three classes restate the question | **Held** — the herd paraphrase maps each class onto one form |
| 6 Only matching commands are executed | **Held** — by the count of unexecuted orders and the never-attempted English design; see the pull in §4 |
| 7 The cone | **Held** for armies and administrations; **Loose** as "always the same in every combination" |
| 8 Power as non-participation | **Held** — it answers "what is power?"; the cone carries it |
| 9 All who take part are the force | **Held if** — held by the job *rulers' private lives leave no trace in the movement*, a job he added |
| 10 "It is a law" | **Loose** — swap for "necessity" or "structure" and nothing moves; see the gauge in §4 |
| 11 Commensurate force | **Held** — by the job of ruling out heroes, wheels and smoke at once; its pictures are loose |
| 12 Justifications precede and release | **Held** — by the Crusade cessation: with a clear aim and no unknown cause, the people did not go |
| 13 Bow-wave on the ship | **Held** — by the job *why we mistake the justification for the cause* |
| 14 History studies the presentation | **Fixed** — he sets what history's subject is; it was not tested |
| 15 The plasterers | **Idle** — the same chapter's argument rebukes the naturalists without it. I checked pairs; it can go |

## Whole-explanation checks

**Flip.** Whatever happened, some wish is found alongside it — the bow-wave. His own guard is real and checkable: the Crusade cessation, and the unexecuted orders. Without those two the account would explain any outcome.

**Direction.** This is the strongest thing here. Poke the order: the event does not move. Poke the event: an order appears alongside. He runs this test himself and gets the right answer.

**Answer hidden in the starting points.** Chapter III assumes the movement is *one* thing wanting *one* commensurate force, then "finds" that force. The unity is a premise, not a result. He is honest about the rest: "we say it is a law because it is inconceivable otherwise."

**Where the jobs came from.** Given: the movements, the Crusade stopping, the historians' contradictions, the unexecuted orders. Added by me: *a movement with no decree at all* (a bank run, a migration). The account covers it and it kills the decree story. Added by him: *the ruler's private life leaves no mark on the nation* — a fair job, and one he wrote himself.

**Pairs that pull.** (a) "Only matching orders are executed" against "many orders are unexecuted." What counts as matching is only knowable after the outcome, so the rule postdicts and barely predicts; his one predicting case is thin. (b) Chapter IX opens by saying history should *deduce* freedom and necessity from the phenomena, then *applies* three factors to them.

**Catch-all and gauge.** Part 10 swallows "why war occurs — we do not know." It has a gauge, though a rough one: if a historian made a *present-day* event fully inevitable, or an ancient one freely chosen, that would worry him. Thin, but stated.

**Rival.** "Movements follow the harvest, prices and disease; leaders and phrases are read off afterwards." Nothing on his change list separates it from his account. At this level they are one explanation. A finer question — which of the mass's conditions fixes the direction — would separate them, and he never asks it.

**Where the parts came from.** *Fitted:* the cone, from the armies and offices he had seen; the three considerations of Chapter IX, from reported moral and legal cases. *Built:* the direction claim — it says what a poke would show. *Asserted:* "every combination," "all cases without exception," "it is a law." *Borrowed:* the will subject to statistical law, and the consciousness of freedom.

## What would make it harder to vary

1. A single case where a clear aim is present and the mass still moves (killing the Crusade stop), or where a ruler's diary visibly traces a nation's movement.
2. A small group — a two-person boat, a family — where the one who works most also decides most. That breaks "always the same" and forces him to state his range.

## What this does not show

Passing is not truth. A loose part may still be right. A true explanation can be guessed for bad reasons and pass anyway.

## One next step

Put the range in writing. Say whether the cone holds "in every combination" or "in large ones," and name what would show the line is drawn in the wrong place.
